title: Present Simple - Formation et emploi
content: Le Present Simple exprime les habitudes, les vérités générales et les états permanents. Formation : sujet + base verbale (+ s à la 3e personne du singulier). I/You/We/They work. He/She/It works. Négation : sujet + do/does + not + base verbale. He does not (doesn't) work. Question : Do/Does + sujet + base verbale? Does he work? Marqueurs de temps : always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day/week.
learning_objectives: Maîtriser la méthode: Present Simple - Formation et emploi

title: Present Continuous - Formation et emploi
content: Le Present Continuous (ou Progressive) exprime une action en cours au moment où l'on parle. Formation : sujet + BE (am/is/are) + verbe-ING. I am working. She is reading. They are playing. Négation : sujet + BE + not + verbe-ING. He is not (isn't) working. Question : BE + sujet + verbe-ING? Are you listening? Marqueurs : now, at the moment, right now, currently. Attention : certains verbes d'état ne s'emploient pas au continuous (like, want, know, believe).
learning_objectives: Maîtriser la méthode: Present Continuous - Formation et emploi

title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous
content: Present Simple : habitudes, routines, vérités générales. 'I play football every Saturday' (habitude). 'Water boils at 100°C' (vérité). Present Continuous : action en cours maintenant. 'I am playing football right now' (en ce moment). Comparaison : 'She works in a bank' (son métier, permanent) vs 'She is working at home today' (exceptionnellement, temporaire). Le choix dépend si l'action est habituelle/permanente (Simple) ou temporaire/en cours (Continuous).
learning_objectives: Maîtriser la méthode: Present Simple vs Present Continuous

title: Past Simple (Preterit) - Verbes réguliers
content: Le Past Simple (Preterit) exprime une action passée, terminée, datée. Verbes réguliers : base verbale + ED. I worked, she played, they watched. Règles d'orthographe : verbe en -e → + d (lived), consonne + y → ied (studied), consonne finale doublée si syllabe accentuée (stopped). Négation : sujet + did not (didn't) + base verbale. She didn't work. Question : Did + sujet + base verbale? Did you work? Marqueurs : yesterday, last week/month/year, ago, in 2020.

title: Past Simple - Verbes irréguliers courants
content: Les verbes irréguliers ont une forme passée spécifique à mémoriser. Essentiels : be → was/were, have → had, do → did, go → went, come → came, see → saw, make → made, take → took, get → got, give → gave, know → knew, think → thought, say → said, tell → told, find → found, leave → left, feel → felt, become → became, begin → began, write → wrote, read → read, eat → ate, drink → drank, run → ran, speak → spoke. La forme est la même à toutes les personnes.

title: Present Perfect - Introduction
content: Le Present Perfect relie le passé au présent. Il exprime une expérience de vie ou une action passée avec un résultat présent. Formation : sujet + have/has + participe passé. I have visited Paris. She has finished her homework. Négation : haven't/hasn't + participe passé. Question : Have/Has + sujet + participe passé? Have you ever been to London? Marqueurs : ever (déjà, questions), never (jamais), already (déjà, affirm.), yet (pas encore), just (juste), since/for (depuis).

title: Future avec Will
content: Will exprime le futur pour des prédictions, des décisions spontanées ou des promesses. Formation : sujet + will + base verbale. I will help you. It will rain tomorrow. Forme contractée : I'll, you'll, he'll... Négation : will not (won't) + base verbale. I won't forget. Question : Will + sujet + base verbale? Will you come? Emplois : prédiction ('It will be sunny'), décision immédiate ('I'll answer the phone'), promesse ('I will always love you'), offre ('I'll carry your bag').

title: Future avec Going to
content: Going to exprime une intention ou une prédiction basée sur des indices présents. Formation : sujet + BE (am/is/are) + going to + base verbale. I am going to study medicine. Négation : BE + not + going to. She isn't going to come. Question : BE + sujet + going to? Are you going to travel? Emplois : intention planifiée ('I'm going to visit my grandma this weekend'), prédiction avec indices ('Look at those clouds, it's going to rain'). Will = spontané/général, Going to = planifié/indices.

title: Modal CAN - Capacité et permission
content: CAN exprime la capacité (savoir faire) ou la permission. Formation : sujet + can + base verbale (sans to). I can swim. She can speak French. Négation : cannot (can't). I can't drive. Question : Can + sujet + base verbale? Can you help me? Emplois : capacité ('He can play the guitar'), permission informelle ('You can use my phone'), possibilité ('It can be cold in winter'). Passé : could. 'I could swim when I was 5.' Could est aussi plus poli pour les demandes : 'Could you help me, please?'

title: Modal MUST - Obligation et déduction
content: MUST exprime une obligation forte ou une déduction logique. Formation : sujet + must + base verbale. You must wear a seatbelt. Négation : must not (mustn't) = interdiction. You mustn't smoke here. Question : Must + sujet + base verbale? (rare). Emplois : obligation ('You must do your homework'), interdiction ('You mustn't be late'), déduction ('He must be tired, he worked all day'). Alternative pour obligation : have to (plus courant). 'I have to go now.'

title: Modal SHOULD - Conseil
content: SHOULD exprime un conseil, une recommandation ou ce qui serait bien de faire. Formation : sujet + should + base verbale. You should eat more vegetables. Négation : should not (shouldn't). You shouldn't stay up late. Question : Should + sujet + base verbale? Should I call him? Emplois : conseil ('You should see a doctor'), reproche ('You should have called me'), opinion ('I think we should leave now'). Should est moins fort que must : c'est un conseil, pas une obligation.

title: Les pronoms personnels sujets et compléments
content: Pronoms sujets (avant le verbe) : I (je), you (tu/vous), he (il), she (elle), it (il/elle neutre), we (nous), they (ils/elles). Pronoms compléments (après le verbe ou préposition) : me (me/moi), you (te/toi/vous), him (le/lui), her (la/lui), it (le/la/lui), us (nous), them (les/leur). Exemples : 'I love her' (je l'aime), 'She loves me' (elle m'aime), 'Give it to them' (donne-le-leur). Le pronom complément suit toujours le verbe ou la préposition.

title: Les adjectifs possessifs
content: Les adjectifs possessifs précèdent le nom et indiquent la possession. My (mon/ma/mes), your (ton/ta/tes, votre/vos), his (son/sa/ses - possesseur masculin), her (son/sa/ses - possesseur féminin), its (son/sa/ses - neutre), our (notre/nos), their (leur/leurs). En anglais, l'adjectif possessif s'accorde avec le possesseur, pas avec l'objet possédé. 'His mother' (sa mère, à lui), 'Her father' (son père, à elle). 'Their books' (leurs livres).

title: There is / There are - Existence
content: There is/are exprime l'existence ou la présence de quelque chose. There is + singulier/indénombrable : 'There is a book on the table.' 'There is some milk.' There are + pluriel : 'There are three cats in the garden.' Négation : There isn't / There aren't. 'There isn't any water.' Question : Is there / Are there? 'Is there a bank near here?' 'Are there any questions?' Passé : There was (singulier), There were (pluriel).

title: Poser des questions - Mots interrogatifs
content: Mots interrogatifs (WH-questions) : What (quoi, quel), Who (qui), Where (où), When (quand), Why (pourquoi), How (comment). Structure : WH-word + auxiliaire + sujet + verbe? 'What do you want?' 'Where does she live?' 'Why are you late?' How + adjectif : How old (quel âge), How much/many (combien), How often (à quelle fréquence), How long (combien de temps), How far (à quelle distance). Yes/No questions : auxiliaire en premier. 'Do you like pizza?' 'Is she French?'

title: Comparatives - Comparatifs
content: Comparatives are used to compare two things or people. Short adjectives (1-2 syllables): add -er + than. Examples: tall -> taller than (My brother is taller than me), fast -> faster than, big -> bigger than (double final consonant), easy -> easier than (y becomes i). Long adjectives (3+ syllables): use more + adjective + than. Examples: beautiful -> more beautiful than (Paris is more beautiful than expected), expensive -> more expensive than, interesting -> more interesting than. Irregular comparatives: good -> better than, bad -> worse than, far -> farther/further than. For equality: as + adjective + as (She is as tall as her sister). For inferiority: not as + adjective + as OR less + adjective + than. Common mistakes: Never say more taller or more better. Pronunciation: than is often pronounced with a weak vowel sound.
typical_questions: How do we form comparatives?
When do we use more?
What are the irregular comparatives?
common_errors: Using more with short adjectives (more big)
Forgetting to double consonants (biger instead of bigger)
learning_objectives: Form comparatives with short adjectives
Form comparatives with long adjectives
Use irregular comparatives correctly

title: Superlatives - Superlatifs
content: Superlatives compare one thing to all others in a group (3+). They express the highest degree. Short adjectives: the + adjective + -est. Examples: tall -> the tallest (He is the tallest in the class), fast -> the fastest, big -> the biggest (double consonant), easy -> the easiest (y becomes i). Long adjectives: the most + adjective. Examples: beautiful -> the most beautiful (It's the most beautiful city), expensive -> the most expensive, interesting -> the most interesting. Irregular superlatives: good -> the best, bad -> the worst, far -> the farthest/furthest. The article THE is always used before superlatives. We often add in/of after superlatives: the best in the world, the tallest of all. For inferiority: the least + adjective (the least expensive option). Note: Superlatives compare 3+ items; comparatives compare only 2. Common pattern: This is the -est / most + adjective + noun + I have ever + past participle. Example: This is the best movie I have ever seen.
typical_questions: How do we form superlatives?
When do we use the most?
What's the difference between comparative and superlative?
learning_objectives: Form superlatives correctly
Use THE with superlatives
Distinguish superlatives from comparatives

title: Relative pronouns - Pronoms relatifs
content: Relative pronouns introduce relative clauses that give more information about a noun. WHO is used for people: The man who lives next door is a teacher. That's the girl who won the competition. WHICH is used for things and animals: The book which I'm reading is interesting. The cat which is sleeping is mine. THAT can replace who or which in defining clauses: The man that lives next door (= who). The book that I'm reading (= which). THAT is more common in spoken English. WHERE is used for places: The house where I was born. This is the school where I study. WHEN is used for time: I remember the day when we met. Defining vs non-defining clauses: Defining clauses are essential to identify the noun (no commas): The girl who is wearing red is my sister. Non-defining clauses add extra information (with commas): My sister, who lives in Paris, is a doctor. You cannot use THAT in non-defining clauses.
typical_questions: When do we use who vs which?
Can we use that instead of who?
What's a relative clause?
learning_objectives: Choose the correct relative pronoun

title: Vocabulary - Food and meals
content: Essential food and meal vocabulary. Meals: breakfast (petit dejeuner), lunch (dejeuner), dinner (diner), snack (gouter). Cooking verbs: to cook, to bake, to fry, to boil, to grill, to roast. Common foods - Fruits: apple, banana, orange, strawberry, grape, pear, cherry. Vegetables: carrot, potato, tomato, lettuce, onion, peas, beans. Meat and fish: chicken, beef, pork, lamb, fish, salmon, tuna. Dairy: milk, cheese, butter, yogurt, cream, eggs. Drinks: water, juice, tea, coffee, soda. At the table: plate, glass, knife, fork, spoon, napkin. Useful expressions: I'm hungry (j'ai faim), I'm thirsty (j'ai soif), Would you like some...?, Can I have...?, It's delicious!, I don't like... Countable vs uncountable: bread, rice, sugar, water are uncountable (some water, NOT a water). Use some in affirmative, any in negative/questions: I have some milk. Do you have any eggs?
typical_questions: How do you say dejeuner in English?
What's the difference between some and any?
Name 5 vegetables in English
common_errors: Saying a water instead of some water
learning_objectives: Know meal vocabulary
Name common foods
Use countable/uncountable correctly

title: Vocabulary - Travel and transport
content: Travel and transport vocabulary. Means of transport: car, bus, train, plane (airplane/aeroplane), boat, ship, bicycle (bike), motorcycle, taxi, underground/metro/subway, tram. Prepositions: by car/bus/train/plane/bike (without article), on foot, in a car (inside), on a bus/train/plane (public transport). Places: airport, train station, bus stop, harbour/port, petrol station (UK)/gas station (US). Travel vocabulary: ticket, passport, luggage/baggage, suitcase, boarding pass, delay, to book, to check in. Actions: to take the bus, to catch a train, to miss a flight, to travel, to arrive, to depart. Directions: turn left/right, go straight on, it's on the left/right, next to, opposite, between, behind, in front of. Questions: How do you get to school? I go by bus. How long does it take? It takes 20 minutes. What time does the train leave/arrive? British vs American: underground (UK) = subway (US), petrol (UK) = gas (US), railway (UK) = railroad (US).

What preposition do we use with transport?
How do you give directions in English?
common_errors: Saying by the bus instead of by bus
Confusing on foot and by foot
learning_objectives: Name means of transport
Use correct prepositions

title: Vocabulary - Environment
content: Environment vocabulary. Nature: forest, tree, river, lake, sea, ocean, mountain, beach, desert, field, flower, grass. Animals: wild animals (lion, elephant, tiger, bear, wolf), farm animals (cow, pig, sheep, horse, chicken), pets (dog, cat, rabbit, hamster). Environmental issues: pollution, climate change, global warming, deforestation, endangered species, recycling, waste, rubbish/garbage. Actions: to recycle, to save energy, to protect, to pollute, to waste, to reduce, to reuse. Weather and climate: sunny, rainy, cloudy, windy, stormy, hot, cold, warm, cool. Useful expressions: We should protect the environment. We must save water. Plastic is bad for the planet. Turn off the lights to save energy. Endangered animals might become extinct. The 3 Rs: Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again), Recycle (make new products from waste). This topic connects to geography and science lessons.
typical_questions: How can we protect the environment?
What does endangered mean?
What are the 3 Rs?
learning_objectives: Use environmental vocabulary
Express opinions about ecology
Discuss environmental actions

title: Communication - Expressing opinions
content: Expressing opinions in English. Giving your opinion: I think (that)..., I believe (that)..., In my opinion..., I feel that..., Personally, I..., From my point of view..., As far as I'm concerned... Agreeing: I agree (with you), You're right, That's true, Exactly, Absolutely, I think so too. Disagreeing (politely): I disagree, I don't think so, I'm not sure about that, I see your point but..., I'm afraid I don't agree, That's not how I see it. Asking for opinions: What do you think?, What's your opinion?, Do you agree?, How do you feel about...?, What do you think about...? Giving reasons: Because..., That's why..., The reason is..., For example... Hedging (being less direct): I think..., Maybe..., Perhaps..., It seems to me that..., I suppose... Example dialogue: What do you think about school uniforms? - Personally, I think they're a good idea because everyone looks the same. - I see your point, but I disagree. I believe students should express their personality through their clothes.
typical_questions: How do you say your opinion politely?
How do you agree or disagree?
What expressions introduce an opinion?
common_errors: Using I am agree instead of I agree
learning_objectives: Express opinions in English
Agree and disagree politely
Support opinions with reasons

title: Communication - Describing past events
content: Describing past events and experiences. Time markers for the past: yesterday, last week/month/year, ago (two days ago, a week ago), in 2020, when I was young, once, at that time. Sequencing words: first, then, after that, next, later, finally, in the end. Useful structures: I went to... and saw..., It was (amazing/boring/fun), We had a great time, The best part was when..., I remember when..., I'll never forget... Describing experiences: What happened? - First, we went to the beach. Then we had a picnic. After that, we played volleyball. Finally, we watched the sunset. Using past simple and past continuous together: I was walking home when it started to rain (interrupted action). While I was studying, my phone rang. Giving details: Where did it happen?, When was it?, Who were you with?, What did you do?, How did you feel? Example: Last summer, I went to Spain with my family. We stayed in Barcelona for a week. The weather was beautiful. We visited the Sagrada Familia - it was amazing! I had a wonderful time.
typical_questions: How do you describe what happened?
What words do we use to sequence events?
How do you talk about your holidays?
learning_objectives: Narrate past events clearly
Use sequencing words
Combine past simple and continuous
